prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened the 10^-18 regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I opened with the quantum cascade laser, which I still regard as a textbook invention, but it has attracted support from only one other colleague and I have to weigh that honestly. After reading the openings, the optical lattice clock is the candidate that best meets the criteria I apply: an original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, proposed in 2001-2003 and followed by a first experimental clock), verified by several independent national laboratories, and with a new measurement capability that lets people see things they could not before: relativistic redshifts across centimetres, tests of constant drift, dark-matter searches. It is also the most broadly supported candidate across the committee (six members ranked it, three in the top three), and the support comes from AMO specialists (Kroll, Lindroth) who can judge the priority record better than I can. Two names give a clean configuration, which is rare on this list.
statement.case_against: My reservation is attribution and novelty. The Prize is for the original experiment, not the second discoverer who did it better, and a large part of the case for Jun Ye is record accuracy and stability (and the many-body clock) rather than the original invention; Katori's 2003 proposal and 2005 clock came first, and Lemonde and others also had early lattice-clock ideas. The frequency comb (2005) and ion clocks (2012) were already recognised, so the committee could read this as an incremental continuation of precision metrology, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. If the archival record shows that Ye's contribution is mainly refinement, a one-person or differently composed prize would be more defensible.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as the clearest case of a new measurement capability changing what can be observed, with Katori proposing the concept and Ye delivering leading accuracy, and he places the quantum cascade laser seventh as more engineering than fundamental physics, with the Kazarinov-Suris priority problem.
responses.response: I agree with the first point and it moved me. His argument is the same one I make for instruments that open a door, and he makes it for a candidate I had underweighted. On the quantum cascade laser I partly disagree: an invention is an invention, and engineering is not disqualifying under the Nobel will. But his priority concern is fair. A 1971 proposal is prior art for the idea, though the 1994 device was a real experimental step, and a committee that must be absolutely sure of the original work would need a careful archival check before crediting Cho as well. That uncertainty, together with the thin support, is why I no longer lead with it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first, as a clean and original magic-wavelength idea with systematic-error-controlled precision, reproduced across RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, and she notes the SI second redefinition roadmap relies on these clocks.
responses.response: Her point on independent reproduction is what settles maturity for me. Her uncertainty about the early priority split is exactly my own, and I would like it checked in the original 2001-2003 papers before we finalise the pair, specifically whether Ye's contribution is the invention or the refinement. I do not think we should wait for the redefinition of the second: the Prize is for the discovery or invention, and the verification is already in hand.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Kane, Mele and Molenkamp first as a clean theory-plus-experiment story with a Z2 invariant, protected edge states and nearly twenty years of independent confirmation, while acknowledging that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D discoveries lie outside the credited set.
responses.response: I ranked this fourth and agree on maturity: there is no question of readiness. My disagreement is about attribution. Molenkamp's group did the original experiment, but the HgTe route was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, so the experimental half of this prize rests on a prediction whose authors would be left out, and Zhang's death means that gap cannot be closed. I do not think it is a fatal flaw, and it is the strongest alternative to the clock. But with a two-name clean configuration available, I would not choose the contested attribution first. I also note that the practical benefit is still prospective.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind essentially all superconducting quantum processors, original and far-reaching, but he states that he directs a programme built on it, and accepts that the 2025 prize is adjacent and that a three-person cap leaves out Blais or Girvin.
responses.response: I value the candidate as an instrument-based advance and ranked it fifth. His disclosure is appropriate, and I would give his technical judgement on distinctness from the 2025 prize real weight while not letting his ranking drive the outcome. My reservations are the adjacency to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits and the fact that any three of the four names leaves out someone decisive; the experimental demonstration by Wallraff and Schoelkopf and the Blais-Girvin theory are tightly interlocked.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as the opening of neutrino astronomy and a clue from nature, with Halzen as the single name, but concedes that credit in a very large collaboration and the role of DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers cannot be resolved here.
responses.response: I find the science compelling, and a new observational window is the kind of door-opening I admire, but I cannot support it at this stage. A single credited name for a discovery made by a collaboration of hundreds is the situation in which I would not be absolutely sure we had identified the people who did the original work, and the source-identification picture is still developing. If the committee wants to go in that direction, we would need expert reports on who conceived the detector concept and who led the first diffuse-flux analysis, not only on Halzen's leadership.

uncertainties: Whether Jun Ye's credit is for the original lattice-clock invention or for later accuracy and stability records, and whether the 2001-2003 priority record supports crediting Katori alone or alongside Ye.

Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a separate achievement from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes or as incremental, and whether it should wait for the redefinition of the second.
Whether the 2D/3D topological-insulator attribution (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) can be made fair with three names, since that is the strongest alternative.

Whether the quantum cascade laser's priority history (Kazarinov and Suris 1971; other Bell Labs co-inventors) leaves a defensible three-person credit, since I would revisit it if an archival check was favourable.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred candidate (B051). For transparency, my colleague Goran Johansson is at Chalmers Physics and has disclosed a stake in B038; I share a department-level affiliation with him but no joint work on circuit QED that I am aware of from my profile, so I would not recuse myself on any shortlisted candidate. I have long-running exchanges with the Japanese microscopy community, but no link to Katori or RIKEN is documented.
